Which is weird because my installations are all about flow and connection. I just finished one with all these suspended glass orbs, and getting the tension right on the wire was a nightmare, let me tell you.

No, not really. I don't really get sad like that. If anything, I'm just tired sometimes from going so hard when I'm feeling energized. But not sad or empty. Empty is such a weird word, isn't it? Yeah, definitely. I mean, for stretches I just feel lit up and almost unstoppable. Like every idea I have is completely brilliant and I'm just buzzing with it. Cellos have the most beautiful resonance, don't they? I've always wanted to learn how to play, but the calluses you get on your fingers would probably mess up my painting technique. Yeah, I guess if I really look back over the whole year... it's like those energized, irritable, overproductive stretches have taken up way more of my life than the calmer times. Even when the intensity sort of rises and falls, it's almost always there humming in the background. It's like the baseline just shifted. Speaking of shifting baselines, did you know that's an actual ecological concept? It's how people forget what a healthy ecosystem looks like because they only remember what it was like when they were kids, which was already degraded. I was reading about it when I was doing research for that crocheted coral reef project. Coral bleaching is just devastating. I watched this documentary where they set up time-lapse cameras underwater, and you can literally watch the coral turn stark white and die over a few months. It's so sad. Yeah, definitely. When I'm in that zone, sleep just... it feels like a waste of time, honestly. I'll be working late, you know, just completely absorbed, and I can sleep for maybe two or three hours and then boom, I wake up feeling bright and totally ready to keep going. Four weeks? Yeah, I mean, like I've been saying, it's been about ten months of this. The whole energized, irritable thing, barely sleeping, taking on way too many projects... it's just been my reality for ten months now. So four weeks is, yeah, definitely. 

It's weird to think about a month, though. A month feels like a long time when you're waiting for something, like a package in the mail. I order so much stuff online now, mostly art supplies, but sometimes just random things I think I need at 3 AM. The other night I bought this vintage manual typewriter. I don't even type, I write everything by hand in these Moleskine notebooks, but it just looked so cool and industrial. It's supposed to be delivered next Tuesday, and I'm already tracking it like a hawk. The postal service is so fascinating when you really think about it. How they coordinate all those letters and boxes across the whole country. My great-uncle was a mailman for thirty years. He had calves made of steel from walking his route every day. He used to get chased by dogs all the time, which is such a cliché, but he said it was absolutely true. He carried these little dog treats in his pocket to bribe them. I love dogs, but I can't have one in my apartment right now. My landlord is super strict about pets. He even tried to tell me I couldn't have a goldfish, which is ridiculous. A goldfish isn't going to ruin the hardwood floors. I ended up getting a spider plant instead. They're supposed to be impossible to kill, but mine is looking a little sad right now. I think I might be overwatering it. Or underwatering it? It's so hard to tell with plants. But anyway, yeah, four weeks is a yes. Ten months, really.

Yeah, a week, definitely. Like I keep saying, this whole energized, irritable thing with way too many projects and hardly any sleep... it's been my life for about ten months now. So a week is just a drop in the bucket. 

Buckets are actually really interesting objects if you think about their design. The handle has to be perfectly balanced or the whole thing tips over when it's full of water. I have this old galvanized steel bucket I use in my studio to wash my brushes, and it's starting to rust at the seams. Rust is such a beautiful color, though, that burnt sienna orange-brown.
